catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry. 2002. Gela. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds), The Oceanic Languages, 525-537. Richmond: Curzon. (archive.org djvu scanned text, local cache)
catalog_quote: 1.3 Stress Stress is applied to the penultimate syllable of the word. With the addition of morphological material after a root, the penultimate syllable of the actual root may be unstressed. When two identical vowels arise word-finally with an intervening morpheme boundary, the resulting sequence is pronounced as a single stressed vowel. Thus compare /'tolu/ ‘three’ with /kolu-u/ ‘with me’ > /ko'lu/.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in both held Crowley 2002 excerpts at section 1.3, p.526. Deciding source is a 2002 linguist-authored grammar sketch (Curzon Oceanic Languages volume) with an explicit stress section — short, single-consultant, but the most recent professional description; Codrington 1885 p.523 (fetched sources now to independently gives penultimate accent for Florida/Gela, so two sources 117 years apart agree and nothing suggests the penultimate coding is wrong. The one work that could deepen the record is Miller 1975 (609 pp SOAS PhD, syntax-focused, stress coverage unverified, not reachable from our machine).
